item.research_question: Can a hierarchical architecture involving secondary nanoprecipitates form inside primary nanoprecipitates in high-entropy alloys, and can an ultrahigh strength be achieved through a high density of such intragranular hierarchical nanoprecipitates?
item.processing_route: Mechanical alloying (MA) for 49 hours (45h dry + 4h wet with ethanol) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1000°C, 30 MPa pressure, 90°C/min heating rate, and <8 Pa vacuum.
item.test_conditions: Room temperature uniaxial tension using in situ SEM microtensile testing with a nominal strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; in situ TEM compression tests at room temperature with an axial displacement rate of 3 nm s–1.
key_findings: Tensile yield strength (σ0.2) of ~1.86 GPa and ultimate tensile strength of ~2.52 GPa at room temperature.
Failure strain of ~5.2% achieved alongside the ultrahigh strength values.
Microstructure consists of a primary fcc phase (~82.3 vol %) and a small amount of bcc phase (~17.7 vol %).

The fcc matrix contains a high density of hierarchical intragranular nanoprecipitates: primary γ′ (L12 structure, ~57 nm avg diameter, ~62 vol % in fcc) and secondary γ* (A1 structure, several nm to tens of nm).
Average spacing between adjacent γ′ nanoprecipitates is ~11 nm.
Dislocations were observed to shear both the primary γ′ and secondary γ* precipitates during in situ TEM compression.
Grain diameters average ~409 nm for the fcc phase and ~227 nm for the bcc phase.
item.mechanism: The ultrahigh strength is primarily attributed to precipitation strengthening via the shearing mechanism, where dislocations shear both the primary coherent γ′ precipitates and the secondary coherent γ* precipitates, creating an 'exaggerated precipitation strengthening effect' due to the hierarchical obstacle distribution. Additional contributions come from grain-boundary strengthening (due to submicrometer grains) and load transfer via the hard bcc phase.
item.limitations: The chemical composition of the secondary γ* precipitates could not be obtained due to their very small sizes.
item.future_work: The authors suggest the design strategy provides insight for achieving ultrahigh strength in HEAs or other multicomponent alloys, implying further exploration of hierarchical architectures, though specific future experiments are not explicitly detailed beyond the general validation of the strategy.
quotes: Here, we report a strategy for the design and fabrication of HEAs that can achieve ultrahigh tensile strengths.

Our results show that precipitation strengthening, as one of the main strengthening mechanisms, contributes to a tensile yield strength (σ0.2) of ~1.86 GPa and an ultimate tensile strength of ~2.52 GPa at room temperature.
γ* nanoprecipitates act as an additional obstacle, which results in an exaggerated precipitation strengthening effect.
